item.title: Canada Imposes New Tariffs on U.S. Goods, as Trade War Intensifies
item.description: The duties are a retaliation against President Trump’s recent tariffs, raising concerns about further escalation.
item.dc:creator: Tony Romm
item.media:credit: Todd Korol for The New York Times
item.media:description: A shipment of Montana lumber last week in Canada, where it will be used to build beehives.

item.title: Near the Border, Americans Fear Losing Ties With Canadians
item.description: Americans in border regions have had symbiotic relationships with Canadians, but the trade war is testing their bonds.
item.dc:creator: Lauren McGaughy
item.media:description: Blaine, Wash., a border town, has had a close relationship with Canadians in the past. But tensions have risen since President Trump imposed tariffs last year.

item.title: Canadian Jet Maker Is Target in Trump’s Trade War
item.description: Montreal-based Bombardier has been embroiled in U.S. trade disputes before. President Trump threatened to bar the company from selling in the United States.
item.dc:creator: John Yoon
item.media:description: Planes in production on the factory floor at a Bombardier plant in Mississauga, Ontario, in 2024.

item.title: Why Stocks Are Defying Gravity and What Could Bring Them Down
item.description: Investors are focused on strong corporate earnings and A.I., while looking past the war in Iran. But rising interest rates are an increasing risk to the rally.
item.dc:creator: Aruni Soni

item.title: Why the Pentagon Is Doing Polygraphs, and Officials Prepare to Release Huge Set of 9/11 Documents
item.description: Plus, could crushable concrete stop the next plane crash?
item.dc:creator: Will Jarvis, Margaret Kadifa, Jake Lucas, Ian Stewart and Adam Satariano
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Jared Soares for The New York Times
item.media:description: U.S. government investigators are subjecting roughly 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests, according to officials briefed on the move.

item.title: Chinese Ship Takes Arctic Shortcut: Smart Business? Or a Political Flex?
item.description: Melting ice is opening a trade route through the Arctic. China has begun the first regular service, part of its polar ambitions.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Gettleman, Jenny Gross and Lily Kuo

item.title: China’s Surging Exports Loom Over Trump’s Talks With Xi
item.description: China’s exports grew by a quarter in the month of August, weeks before its leader, Xi Jinping, is set to meet with President Trump in Washington.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Stevenson
item.media:description: Containers at a port in Nanjing, China, on Monday. Some of the demand for Chinese goods globally has been driven by a voracious appetite to build out artificial intelligence capabilities.

item.title: Roger Marshall Sued 700 Patients for Debts; 81 Were Arrested. Now He’s a Senator.
item.description: Patients sued by Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas were routinely charged 18 percent interest, The Times found. Some had bank accounts garnished.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Kliff
item.media:description: Senator Roger Marshall spent 25 years practicing obstetrics before running for Congress.

item.title: Saudi Arabia Vows Retaliation After Houthi Attacks Injure Dozens
item.description: The latest escalation threatens to drag Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia back into a full-blown war.
item.dc:creator: Qasim Nauman and Vivian Nereim
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:description: Members of the Houthi security force standing guard in Sanaa, Yemen, in July.

item.title: Oil Climbs Toward $100 a Barrel Following Houthi Attacks
item.description: Analysts said they expected the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, to remain elevated for the rest of the year.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Friedman
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)

item.title: UK Imposes Sanctions on Israeli Settlements in West Bank, Accuses Settlers of Ethnic Cleansing
item.description: Ed Miliband, the U.K. foreign secretary, said Britain believes there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, and will ban goods from illegal settlements.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Castle, Adam Rasgon, Aaron Boxerman and Isabel Kershner
item.media:description: Palestinian villagers harvesting olives in the village of Turmus Aya, with Israeli settlements in the background, northeast of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank in 2025.

item.title: A.I. Models Built a Computer Worm That Could Rapidly Hack WeChat Accounts
item.description: The attack, discovered by A.I. researchers, could have compromised hundreds of millions of devices within hours, experts said.
item.dc:creator: Dustin Volz
item.media:description: Researchers at Calif, a security company, recently built a hacking tool in a little more than a week that could run roughshod across WeChat, the popular messaging platform.

item.title: A.I. Listings Are So Widespread Even Zillow Is Concerned
item.description: Listing sites are littered with homes with fake fireplaces, improved views and virtual landscaping, raising false advertising concerns.
item.dc:creator: Gerry Smith

item.title: French A.I. Start-Up Mistral Raises $3.5 Billion as Part of Strategy Shift
item.description: Mistral is trying to keep pace with American and Chinese rivals while offering customers a European alternative for artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Adam Satariano
item.media:credit: Stephane De Sakutin/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A Mistral event in Paris in May. The company, which started making artificial intelligence models in 2023, will now also build data centers and other A.I. infrastructure in Europe.

item.title: Top Mathematician Announces New Institute for A.I. Safety
item.description: Jacob Tsimerman, a recent recipient of the Fields Medal, believes that higher mathematics can help curb the dangers of runaway artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: Canadian mathematician Jacob Tsimerman, who has announced the founding of the Mathematical A.I. Safety Institute (MAISI).

item.title: After 9/11, Documents Suggest, New Yorkers Were Misled About Air Quality
item.description: The Mamdani administration is releasing more than 170,000 pages of documents related to the air quality around the World Trade Center site in the months after the Sept. 11 attacks.
item.dc:creator: Sally Goldenberg and Nina Agrawal
item.media:credit: Chang W. Lee/The New York Times
item.media:description: Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.

item.title: 9/11’s Dust and Ash Coated Their Childhood. Is It Still Making Them Ill?
item.description: Much of the research on exposure to the World Trade Center residue has focused on emergency workers, but people there when they were young say their health is at risk, too.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Goldstein
item.media:description: Jacob Fortinsky and Sarah Fortinsky were growing up across from the World Trade Center. The Sept. 11, 2001, attack still casts a shadow.

item.title: AfD’s Far Right Win Puts New Pressure on Germany’s Leader Merz
item.description: Antipathy to Chancellor Friedrich Merz was a reason the far right surged in a state election. Though he does not face a national election until 2029, his leadership is under increasing scrutiny.
item.dc:creator: Jim Tankersley
item.media:description: Friedrich Merz, Germany’s chancellor and the Christian Democratic Union party leader, at a press briefing in Berlin on Monday.

item.title: The Absurd, Unending Quest to Floodproof the New York City Subway
item.description: In an era of heavy rain, a transit system with 47,000 openings is bound to leak.
item.dc:creator: Mark Chiusano
item.media:credit: Hilary Swift for The New York Times
item.media:description: Flooding in Penn Station, Aug. 20. New York City is no longer dealing just with the usual water challenges of the past century. The rain has become worse — a lot worse.

item.title: Don’t Have an Official N.Y.C. Trash Bin? Now It’ll Cost You.
item.description: Residential buildings with fewer than 10 units are required to put out their trash in official “NYC Bins” as part of the city’s efforts to deter rats. Owners who don’t comply will be fined.
item.dc:creator: Emma G. Fitzsimmons
item.media:credit: Emil Salman for The New York Times
item.media:description: The grace period is ending: Residential buildings with nine or fewer units that do not use official city bins for their trash now face fines starting at $50. (Recycling can still be put out in bags.)

item.title: Thieves Steal Artworks From Renoir Museum in France
item.description: Almost a year after the brazen Louvre heist, thieves targeted a museum that was formerly the artist’s home in the south of France.
item.dc:creator: Ségolène Le Stradic
item.media:description: Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s study at his museum in Cagnes-Sur-Mer, France, in 2016. The museum was broken into early Tuesday, and several artworks were stolen.

item.title: Voters Have Spoken. Why Aren’t Democrats Listening?
item.description: Less than two years after a catastrophic election, the Democratic brand remains unpopular, and the party is still in the grip of a divisive identity crisis.
item.dc:creator: Ben Rhodes

item.title: ‘60 Minutes’ Prepares for a High-Pressure Premiere After Its Turbulent Shake-Up
item.description: Nick Bilton, the new executive producer, has begun to put his stamp on the show. Up first: an exclusive interview with an officer who was aboard the F-15 fighter shot down over Iran.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Mullin
item.media:credit: Phelan M. Ebenhack, via Associated Press
item.media:description: A promotion for “60 Minutes” in July in Manhattan. The CBS program’s new season under Nick Bilton, who became executive producer in May, starts on Sunday.
